1401.title: Failure
1401.hook: Peter, Paul, David, Moses all failed badly
1401.howItsDone: Christians bring their failures to God in confession, privately or in a service, and Catholic and Orthodox Christians also confess to a priest and receive absolution; Psalm 51 is used as a prayer of repentance in several liturgies.

segments.voice: Yesterday: God setteth the solitary in families, and from the cross, behold thy mother. Your line was set in families.

A short list of résumés. One man killed someone and fled the country. One took another man's wife, then arranged for the husband to die in battle. One went house to house dragging believers off to prison. One promised he would never deny his friend, and then did, before the cock crowed. Moses. David. Paul. Peter. Scripture writes these moments down in plain sight. And none of their stories stops there.

Peter's story has a strange order. Before the denial, Jesus tells him in Luke: "I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not: and when thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren." The comeback is spoken before the fall. Then Peter denies him, and "Peter went out, and wept bitterly." Later, by the sea in John's Gospel, the risen Jesus asks him, "Lovest thou me?" and gives him a job: "Feed my sheep." Then David. Nathan the prophet tells him of a rich man who steals a poor man's only lamb. David is furious. Then Nathan says it: "Thou art the man." David answers, "I have sinned against the LORD." The heading of Psalm 51 ties it to this moment: "Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me." The story is honest that consequences stay. But it keeps going. Then Moses, whose running you met in year two. He killed a man and ran to Midian. And it was there, keeping someone else's sheep, that the bush burned and the call came. The call found a man who had run. Last, Paul. He never pretends the past didn't happen: "I am the least of the apostles, that am not meet to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God." Then the next sentence: "But by the grace of God I am what I am." Failure is not final doesn't mean failure didn't matter. Peter wept. David's house suffered. But in each story, the failure is a chapter, and the book goes on.
screen: `THE CALL FOUND A MAN WHO RAN.`
`BY THE GRACE OF GOD I AM WHAT I AM.`

segments.voice: Choose one failure you keep replaying, one that still stings, and name it the way Paul named his: this happened, and it was mine. If you can still make it right, set that aside for later; for now, put down the punishment. If you pray, say David's line, create in me a clean heart, O God; if you don't, tell yourself plainly: that was a chapter, not the end. If it ever turns into thoughts of harming yourself, call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
Failure. Falling short, sometimes badly. In scripture Moses, David, Paul and Peter all fail, and every one of their stories keeps going.
Your line: failure is not final. Peter wept, and then was given a job. Until tomorrow.

1402.title: Growing old (Psalm 71:9, 18)
1402.hook: don't cast me off in old age; let me tell the next generation
1402.howItsDone: Christians pray for and visit older members of their churches, take communion to people who can no longer come, and in some congregations grandparents and elders pass on the faith by teaching, telling their stories and praying with the young.

segments.voice: Yesterday, failure: Moses, David, Paul and Peter, their worst moments written down in plain sight. Your line was failure is not final.

Gray hair on the pillow. Reading glasses in three rooms of the house. A hand that shakes a little when it pours the coffee. Somewhere in the Psalms is a prayer from someone who has noticed all of this in their own body, and is frightened. Not of dying, exactly. Of being set aside: the person nobody calls, whose stories nobody asks for anymore. The psalm names that fear out loud, then does something unexpected with it. It asks for one more job.

Psalm seventy-one, verse nine, in the King James words: "Cast me not off in the time of old age; forsake me not when my strength faileth." That's the fear, plainly said. The psalm doesn't pretend age is all wisdom and rocking chairs. Strength fails. People drift away. Later in the same psalm, the voice comes back with a request: "Now also when I am old and greyheaded, O God, forsake me not; until I have shewed thy strength unto this generation, and thy power to every one that is to come." Listen to the word until. Don't let me go until I've told them. This old person isn't asking to be kept comfortable, but useful. They carry something the young don't have yet, a long memory of what God has done, and they want to hand it on. Proverbs says, "The hoary head is a crown of glory, if it be found in the way of righteousness." And in Luke's Gospel, when Mary and Joseph bring the baby Jesus to the temple, two people take the child to heart: Simeon, who had been told he would not see death before he saw the Lord's Christ, and Anna, daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Aser, a widow Luke says was of a great age. What does Anna do? She speaks of the child to everyone who looked for redemption in Jerusalem. She tells the next generation. The psalm's picture is simple: the old are not finished. They carry the stories across.
screen: `CAST ME NOT OFF IN OLD AGE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone older than you, a grandparent, a neighbor, someone from church or work, and picture their face. Find one question you've never asked them, what was your hardest year, who taught you to pray, or not to, what do you want us to remember, and simply hold it. If you pray, you can pray the psalm's own words for them: cast them not off.
Growing old. In Psalm seventy-one, it's a fear named honestly, and a calling: to show God's strength to the generation that comes next.
Your line: tell the next generation. In this psalm, gray hair still has work to do. See you tomorrow.

1403.title: When a child dies
1403.hook: the hardest grief; Christians hold it with Rachel weeping and with hope
1403.howItsDone: Christians mourn children with funerals, prayers and the hope of the resurrection; churches hold services of remembrance, some offer support groups for bereaved parents, and traditions differ in how they speak about children who die.

segments.voice: Yesterday, growing old: cast me not off, until I have shewed thy strength. Your line was tell the next generation.

A small coffin is lighter than it should be. Nothing anyone says beside it makes it fit. This lesson goes slowly, and it's fine to stop at any point. If this is your grief, nothing here is meant to explain it away. The Bible doesn't either. It gives a mother's voice, weeping in a town called Ramah, a voice that refuses to be comforted. Christians have kept her voice in their scripture, and they hold this grief beside her.

Her name is Rachel. In Genesis she is the mother of Joseph and Benjamin, and she dies on the road. Later, the prophet Jeremiah hears her again, weeping over her people as they are carried away. In the King James words: "A voice was heard in Ramah, lamentation, and bitter weeping; Rahel weeping for her children refused to be comforted for her children, because they were not." Refused to be comforted. The Bible doesn't scold her. It writes it down. Then Matthew's Gospel picks up the same line, after Herod has the little children of Bethlehem killed: "Rachel weeping for her children, and would not be comforted, because they are not." Right inside the Christmas story, a mother who cannot be consoled. Then a second thing. In Jeremiah, God answers the weeping: "Refrain thy voice from weeping, and thine eyes from tears: for thy work shall be rewarded, saith the LORD." And then, "there is hope in thine end." Weeping, then hope. Not hope instead of weeping. King David, when his infant son dies, says: "I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me." Christian funeral prayers speak of the hope of the resurrection, and some Christians speak of seeing loved ones again. Churches describe that hope in different ways, and some leave the details with God. Both voices stay in the book. The tears are not a failure of faith. In the Bible, they are part of it.

If you know a mother or father who has lost a child, at any age, bring their face to mind; if not, hold the ones you'll never meet, in a hospital tonight or a town at war. Stay with them without reaching for words, the way someone sits beside a person who is crying, and if you pray, simply say Rachel's name and let God fill in the rest. If this grief is your own and it feels too heavy to carry alone, or you're thinking of harming yourself, please call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
When a child dies. The grief the Bible gives to Rachel, who would not be comforted, and the hope held beside it, without taking her tears away.
Your line: rachel weeping. Her tears stay in the book, beside the hope. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1404.title: How long? (Psalm 13)
1404.hook: injustice cries out, and God hears the cry
1404.howItsDone: Christians pray the lament psalms, including Psalm 13, in worship and in private, and churches and Christian groups bring that cry into action through advocacy, legal aid, protest and care for people who are being wronged.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a mother in Ramah who would not be comforted, and hope spoken beside her tears. Your line was rachel weeping.

Two words and a question mark. They're on protest signs and in hospital waiting rooms. A tenant says them about the landlord who won't fix the heat. A family says them about a trial that keeps getting postponed. A child says them in the back seat, and a whole people says them across generations. How long? It sounds like impatience. In the Bible it's something else: a prayer, and a cry about what is wrong. A short psalm asks it again and again, and the Bible keeps answering that the cry is heard.

Back on day one hundred five, this psalm taught that complaint is a prayer too, and not long ago its first line came up as an argument with God. Today, listen for verse two, where a third figure enters, the enemy: "How long shall I take counsel in my soul, having sorrow in my heart daily? how long shall mine enemy be exalted over me?" Someone is winning who shouldn't be. That turns how long from a sigh into a cry about injustice. And the Bible says that kind of cry is heard. From the burning bush, God says in Exodus: "I have surely seen the affliction of my people which are in Egypt, and have heard their cry by reason of their taskmasters; for I know their sorrows." Seen, heard, known, and every word points at people worked by taskmasters. The prophet Habakkuk opens with the same complaint, about violence and judgment gone crooked: "O LORD, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear!" And in Revelation, the souls of those slain for the word of God cry from under the altar: "How long, O Lord, holy and true?" From the psalms to the last book, the question is never thrown out. Then Psalm thirteen ends in a strange place. Nothing outside has changed yet. But the voice says, "But I have trusted in thy mercy; my heart shall rejoice in thy salvation." The cry and the trust come from the same mouth. How long is one of the ways people pray about what's wrong, and keep praying.
screen: `HOW LONG, O LORD, HOLY AND TRUE?`
`BUT I HAVE TRUSTED IN THY MERCY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one wrong that has gone on too long, far away or on your own street: someone underpaid, someone unheard, someone waiting for a hearing that never comes, and name it plainly. If you pray, bring it to God in the psalm's own words, how long, O Lord; if you don't, just hold it in the open, without looking away.
How long? The cry of Psalm thirteen, spoken straight to God when wrong is winning, and kept in scripture as a prayer.
Your line: how long, o lord? In the Bible, that cry is heard, and kept. See you tomorrow.

1405.title: War
1405.hook: Christians pray for peace and for those who fight, and grieve all the dead
1405.howItsDone: Christians pray for peace in public worship, for those in the armed forces and for victims of war; some churches, such as the Mennonites and Quakers, hold to nonviolence, while Catholic teaching and other churches follow the just war tradition, and Christians on both sides run relief work for refugees and the wounded.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the cry of Psalm thirteen. Your line was how long, o lord?

On a Sunday morning, in a church in a country at war, the prayers reach the part where the names are read. A soldier's mother sits in the third row. Two rows back sits a family who fled the fighting with one suitcase. In some churches, the prayers that morning ask for peace, for those who serve, for the wounded, for the leaders, and, following Jesus's words about loving enemies, for the enemy. All in one breath. It's a hard place to stand, and a hard question for the faith.
screen: `A CHURCH IN A COUNTRY AT WAR.`

segments.voice: Begin with the hope. Isaiah sees a day when the nations "shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks: nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more." Weapons melted into farm tools. A psalm says of God, "He maketh wars to cease unto the end of the earth; he breaketh the bow, and cutteth the spear in sunder." Here, war is not how things are meant to be. Then Jesus, on a hillside: "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God." Not the peace lovers. The peacemakers. Peace is something you make, often at a cost. Christians have answered a world at war in different ways. Some churches, like the Mennonites and the Quakers, hold that followers of Jesus should not take up arms at all, pointing to his words about loving enemies and turning the other cheek. Others, including the Catholic Church and a number of Protestant churches, follow the just war tradition, linked with Augustine and Thomas Aquinas: war may sometimes be permitted, only for a just cause such as protecting the innocent, only as a last resort, and always under strict limits. And there's a small scene in Luke. Soldiers ask John the Baptist what they should do. He doesn't tell them to leave the army. He says, "Do violence to no man, neither accuse any falsely; and be content with your wages." Across all these answers, the dead on both sides are still someone's children. Christians who disagree about war can still pray at the same graveside.

Bring to mind one war happening now, and picture one ordinary person on each side: someone in uniform, someone sheltering in a basement. Then picture the ones who would be called the enemy, and hold them too. If you pray, you can pray Isaiah's line for all of them, that nation shall not lift up sword against nation; if you don't, simply hold them in your heart.
War. In Isaiah's hope, something to be beaten into plowshares; for Christians, something they answer in different ways, while grieving every life it takes.
Your line: blessed are the peacemakers. Jesus says they shall be called the children of God. Until tomorrow.

1406.title: Disasters
1406.hook: after earthquakes and floods, Christians give, rebuild and lament
1406.howItsDone: After disasters, churches open their buildings as shelters and supply centers, hold services of lament, collect money through their relief agencies, and send volunteers to clean up and rebuild homes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, war: swords into plowshares, and Christians answering it in different ways. Your line was blessed are the peacemakers.

The water has gone down, and it left a line on every wall at the same height. Mud in the kitchen drawers. Photographs drying on a fence. A church parking lot turned into a warehouse of bottled water and diapers, strangers in work gloves passing boxes hand to hand. After a flood, an earthquake, a fire, the same question comes up on the news and at kitchen tables: why did God let this happen? The Bible doesn't give a tidy answer. But it does show what people of faith do next.

First, Jesus refuses one answer. In Luke, he himself brings up a tower that fell in Jerusalem: "Or those eighteen, upon whom the tower in Siloam fell, and slew them, think ye that they were sinners above all men that dwelt in Jerusalem? I tell you, Nay." The people under the tower weren't being punished for being worse than everyone else. Whatever a disaster is, the text won't let anyone point at the victims. Then there's lament. Lamentations is a set of poems over a ruined city, and in the middle of the wreckage one line holds on: "It is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness." Then there's giving. In Acts, a prophet named Agabus warns that a famine is coming, and the response is: "Then the disciples, every man according to his ability, determined to send relief unto the brethren which dwelt in Judaea." Not a debate about why. A collection. Then rebuilding. Nehemiah stands before the broken walls of Jerusalem and says, "Come, and let us build up the wall." The people answer, "Let us rise up and build." Lament, give, rebuild. Churches today hold services of mourning after disasters, collect relief, and send crews to tear out wet drywall. The why may never be answered. The text keeps pointing at the next morning, and the next brick.

Bring to mind one place hit recently by a flood, a storm, an earthquake or a fire, and picture one family standing in a doorway there. Hold them for a while without trying to explain anything. If you pray, you can pray the line from Lamentations over them, that his compassions fail not; if you don't, let them stay in your thoughts a little longer.
Disasters. Floods, quakes and fires that the Bible won't blame on the victims, met with lament, with relief, and with people rising up to build.
Your line: rebuild. In Nehemiah, the people answered, let us rise up and build. Same time tomorrow.

1407.title: Hope
1407.hook: hope that is seen is not hope (Romans 8:24)
1407.howItsDone: Christians speak of hope in the resurrection at funerals, in the creeds and in prayers for the sick and the dying, and churches mark it each year at Easter and in the waiting season of Advent.

segments.voice: Yesterday, disasters: the tower in Siloam, mercies new every morning, and Nehemiah's let us rise up and build. Your line was rebuild.

These have been heavy days. Failure. Growing old. A child's death. How long, O Lord. War. Floods and earthquakes. One hard room after another. Now, at the end of it, one word Christians set against all of it. Not as a bandage. As a direction. Paul wrote about it to the Christians in Rome, and defined it in a way that sounds, at first, like a riddle: hope that is seen is not hope.
screen: `HOPE THAT IS SEEN IS NOT HOPE.`

segments.voice: Here is the riddle in full, in the King James words: "For we are saved by hope: but hope that is seen is not hope: for what a man seeth, why doth he yet hope for? But if we hope for that we see not, then do we with patience wait for it." Nobody hopes for the sunrise once the sun is up. You only hope for what isn't here yet. So hope, in Paul's sense, isn't a mood that comes when things look good. It's what you hold when they don't. And look where Paul says this. A few lines earlier he describes the whole world in pain: "For we know that the whole creation groaneth and travaileth in pain together until now." Travaileth: the old word for labor, for giving birth. Paul doesn't pretend the groaning isn't real. He hears it as labor pains, pain that is going somewhere. That's the shape of hope in this chapter. Not optimism, the guess that things will probably work out. In Paul's letter it's trust in a promise that God will finish what he started, and for Christians the resurrection of Jesus is the first sign of it. Paul's example is Abraham, who "against hope believed in hope." Against all the evidence, he kept hoping. And the letter to the Hebrews ties hope to faith: "Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen." In Paul's letter, every one of those hard rooms has that unseen thing at the far end. Not a door anyone can see yet. A door Christians trust is there.
screen: `HOPE THAT IS SEEN IS NOT HOPE.`

segments.voice: Look back over the last few days, failure, age, grief, injustice, war, disaster, and choose the one that stayed with you most. Name one thing you hope for in it that you can't see yet, a healing, a reconciliation, a peace, and hold it like a seed in a closed hand, without arguing about how likely it is. If you pray, you can offer it to God in Paul's words, that we hope for that we see not.
Hope. In Paul's letter, the trust that holds on to what isn't seen yet, the way a woman in labor holds on to a child she hasn't met.
Your line: hope unseen. In Paul's letter, it's held hardest when things look finished. See you tomorrow.
